results.result: Recent experimental studies have identified key brainstem structures (CnF, PPN, LPGi) involved in locomotor control, but the exact pathways and circuit organization remain unclear. Glutamatergic neurons in CnF and PPN contribute to slow locomotion, while only CnF glutamatergic neurons elicit fast locomotion. These neurons project to the LPGi and activate spinal circuits. Inhibitory neurons in these regions can reduce or halt locomotion.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C19 establish the experimental background from prior work (C1, C9-C18) and identify the knowledge gap (C2, C19) that motivates the current study. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to experimental studies (Capelli et al., 2017; Caggiano et al., 2018; Josset et al., 2018) and represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: The model proposes that brainstem control of locomotion operates through two distinct pathways: one controlling locomotor speed via connections to rhythm generating circuits (RGs), and another controlling gait via connections to commissural interneurons (CINs) and long propriospinal neurons (LPNs). The model extends previous work by incorporating brainstem circuits (CnF, PPN, LPGi) and their descending pathways to the spinal cord.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C20-C22, C71-C72, C78-C79 present the central hypothesis and main result of the study. The two-pathway model is supported by simulation results (C22, C48) that reproduce experimental observations. The model architecture is clearly described (C21, C24-C37) and builds logically on previous modeling work (C3, C20, C71-C72). The suggestion of two distinct LPGi glutamatergic populations (C31, C78) is a testable hypothesis that emerges from the modeling.

results.result: The computational model consists of four rhythm generators (RGs) controlling each limb, interacting via CINs and LPNs. The brainstem component includes bilaterally located CnF and PPN (MLR) and LPGi (RF) structures with glutamatergic and GABAergic/glycinergic neurons. A key hypothesis is that each LPGi contains two distinct glutamatergic populations (LPGi-Glu-1 and LPGi-Glu-2) mediating separate pathways for frequency and gait control.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C39, C116-C119 describe the model architecture and implementation. The model structure is clearly documented with connectivity patterns based on experimental data (C27-C30 cite Caggiano et al., 2018; Capelli et al., 2017). The hypothesis of two distinct LPGi populations (C31) is explicitly stated as a model assumption. Model parameters and implementation details are provided (C38, C116-C119), and the model is made available on GitHub for reproducibility.

results.result: Model simulations of unilateral stimulation of glutamatergic neurons in CnF, PPN, and LPGi reproduce key experimental observations. CnF stimulation produces a wide frequency range (up to 10-11 Hz) with all four gaits (walk, trot, gallop, bound). PPN stimulation produces only lower frequencies (~8 Hz) with alternating gaits (walk, trot). LPGi stimulation produces effects similar to CnF stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48, C90-C95 present simulation results that are directly compared to experimental data from Caggiano et al. (2018), Josset et al. (2018), and Capelli et al. (2017). The model successfully reproduces the differential effects of CnF vs. PPN stimulation (C43, C45, C90, C92) and the similarity between CnF and LPGi stimulation (C47, C94). Results are shown in Figures 3 and 5 and are described as consistent with experimental findings (C44, C48, C91, C93, C95).

results.result: Model simulations predict that bilateral inactivation of the PPN during CnF-evoked locomotion shifts the transition from alternating gaits (trot) to synchronized gaits (gallop/bound) toward lower locomotor frequencies. This shift is accompanied by increased variability in left-right phase differences and a wider transition period between gaits. The model reproduces the experimental observation that animals can still express the full spectrum of gaits after PPN inactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C49-C51, C53-C54, C96-C99 present a key prediction of the model regarding PPN inactivation. The mechanism is clearly explained (C50): PPN projects only to LPGi-Glu-1 (frequency control), so its inactivation reduces frequency drive while leaving LPGi-Glu-2 (gait control) unaffected. Results are shown in Figure 4 and are qualitatively consistent with experimental data from Caggiano et al. (2018) showing that animals retain all gaits after PPN inactivation (C97-C98). The prediction of increased variability (C53-C54) is a testable hypothesis.

results.result: Model simulations of inhibitory neuron activation reproduce experimental observations. Unilateral activation of CnF or LPGi inhibitory neurons progressively reduces locomotor frequency through orderly gait transitions and can halt locomotion. PPN inhibitory neuron activation reduces frequency but cannot stop locomotion. The model reveals different mechanisms: CnF inhibitory neurons act locally within the MLR, while LPGi inhibitory neurons suppress downstream spinal targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C70, C100-C107 present simulation results on inhibitory neuron activation that are compared to experimental data from Caggiano et al. (2018) and Capelli et al. (2017). The model reproduces the differential effects of CnF vs. PPN inhibitory neuron activation (C62-C64, C100-C101) and the similarity between CnF and LPGi effects (C65-C66, C104-C105). Results are shown in Figure 6. The model provides mechanistic insight into the different sites of action (C68-C70). The prediction of orderly gait transitions during inhibition (C106-C107) is a testable hypothesis.

results.result: The model focuses on the LPGi as the primary RF nucleus mediating MLR control based on Capelli et al. (2017), but acknowledges that other RF pathways exist and that the model's 'LPGi' may represent a broader population of glutamatergic neurons. The identity and location of these neurons are currently unknown. Similar relay interneurons have been found in cats and rats.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77, C80 discuss the rationale and limitations of focusing on LPGi. The decision is justified by experimental data (C73, citing Capelli et al., 2017), but the authors appropriately acknowledge alternative pathways (C74-C75) and the uncertainty about what the model's LPGi represents (C76-C77). The existence of similar relay neurons in other species (C80) provides supporting evidence for the model's assumptions.

results.result: The model proposes a mechanistic explanation for the differential roles of CnF and PPN in controlling slow vs. fast locomotion. PPN projections target only LPGi-Glu-1 (frequency control), while CnF projections target both LPGi-Glu-1 and LPGi-Glu-2 (frequency and gait control). Additionally, CnF-to-LPGi-Glu-1 synaptic weights are assumed to be stronger than PPN-to-LPGi-Glu-1 weights.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C89 present the model's mechanistic explanation for experimental observations about PPN and CnF function. The differential projection patterns (C87-C88) and synaptic weight assumptions (C89) are clearly stated as model hypotheses. These assumptions allow the model to reproduce the experimental findings that PPN activation produces only slow locomotion with alternating gaits while CnF activation produces the full range of speeds and gaits (C82-C83, C90-C93). The model reconciles apparently conflicting findings from different studies (C84-C86).

results.result: The model implements inhibitory connections from CnF to PPN based on the inference that CnF inhibitory neuron activation can fully suppress locomotion. However, these inhibitory connections have not been shown experimentally.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 present a model assumption (CnF inhibitory connections to PPN) that is inferred from functional data but lacks direct anatomical evidence. While the inference is reasonable (C102), the authors appropriately acknowledge that these connections have not been experimentally demonstrated (C103). This represents a testable prediction of the model that requires experimental validation.

results.result: Background knowledge about locomotor gaits and neural control: Animals exhibit alternating gaits (walk, trot) during slow locomotion and synchronous gaits (gallop, bound) during fast locomotion. Locomotor oscillations are generated in the spinal cord, but speed and gait are controlled by brainstem structures. Vestibulospinal neurons are tonically active, project to extensor pools, and mediate extensor tone.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8, C40-C42 present established background knowledge supported by multiple citations to previous research. These claims provide context for the study but do not represent new findings. All claims are appropriately referenced to prior work.

results.result: The model extends previous work with minimal changes to preserve prior assumptions, but increased complexity limits mathematical analysis. The study focuses on central neural interactions without considering reflex circuits, motoneurons, biomechanics, or heterogeneous neuronal activity. Robustness testing shows the model maintains stable gaits with parameter variations up to σp ≤ 0.04, with 50% of models unstable at σp = 0.2.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C122 describe the modeling approach, limitations, and robustness analysis. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C110, C113-C115) and suggest future directions (C111). Robustness testing (C120-C122) demonstrates that the model is reasonably robust to parameter variations, supporting the conclusion that it represents a 'coarse system' (C122). The limitations are clearly stated and do not undermine the main findings.
